newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end lower, await Greenspan's prose.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end lower, await Greenspan's prose.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed lower as participants played it safe in a light session marked by scattered fears that Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan might deliver a hawkish message to Congress on Tuesday.
The 6.625-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended down 6/32 at 101-2/32. Its yield was at 6.54 percent, against 6.52 on Friday's close.
The powerful Fed Chairman will deliver the first leg of his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on Tuesday to a House Banking subcommittee.
Greenspan will then appear before a Senate banking panel on Wednesday, completing the second leg of the testimony.

Conventional Wall Street wisdom Monday expected Greenspan to say that inflation remained dormant but had not vanished from the U.S. economy. Greenspan was expected to add that central bankers should be wary of that.
"The risks with the testimony are more on the side of disappointment than good news," said Greg Jones, chief economist at consulting firm Briefing.com.
Jones said the two-year note yield, which closed at 5.93 percent, was just about 40 basis points over the target for the federal funds rate, set by the Fed at 5.50 percent.

"Basically, to get much further (than that) you have to start talking about easing at some point. And I don't think anybody really expects Greenspan to give any reason to hope for that tomorrow," Jones said.
Analysts also said the market appeared to be looking for a reason to consolidate gains made over the past few weeks, adding that the Humphrey-Hawkins testimony could work as a timely justification.
"The market is ... looking for an excuse to consolidate and this will be a good excuse to do so," said Cary Leahey, chief U.S. economist at High Frequency Economics Inc.

Pundits said some other factors may have been weighing on prices as well, including recurring jitters about upcoming supply. The Treasury will offer $15.5 billion in two-year notes Tuesday and $11.5 billion in five-year notes Wednesday.
"With a combination of Humphrey-Hawkins and supply, you'll probably trade lower," Leahey said.
Analysts said U.S. debt prices might drop a bit ahead of the fresh supply even though the Treasury appears to be enjoying surging revenues and a shrinking public debt.

On recent rumors that the Treasury might cut the size of the upcoming quarterly refunding effort because of the narrowing deficit, Leahey said, "I would argue that you've had such an explosive rally on the back end ... that you're probably going to trade down before you get to the refunding."

Adding to the market's bearishness on Monday was some hedge fund selling of long-term cash bonds, as well as September futures contracts coupled with some mild retail activity in the middle of the yield spectrum, experts said.
The market showed "decent" demand for the Treasury's sale of $16 billion in three- and six-month bills, which were placed with rates of 5.11 and 5.17 percent, respectively.
"We had decent demand for the bills, but nothing earth- shattering," said a trader at a major investment bank.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed at 5.26 percent. The six-month bill rate was at 5.38 percent. The year bill rate closed at 5.59 percent.
The five-year note traded off 3/32 at 100-11/32 to yield 6.17 percent. The ten-year note closed down 4/32 at 102-20/32, yielding 6.26 percent.
